title: Nani's ten and the phone's ten
hookLine: Nani's ten forms of Vishnu don't match the list on Priya's phone
tomorrow: one name in the ten is still written 'will be.' which one?

cards: Every family has the recipe, and every aunt's version of the recipe is different.

Priya takes Dawa's question to Nani, who counts on her fingers without looking up from the stove: fish, tortoise, boar, man-lion, dwarf, Parashurama, Rama, Balarama, Krishna, Kalki. Priya checks the list on her phone.
Fish, tortoise, boar, man-lion, dwarf, Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, Buddha, Kalki. Same ten fingers, a different name on one of them. And Nani, stirring, isn't bothered at all.

teach.b: Start with the Bhagavata. Its first list doesn't stop at ten. It names Balarama and Krishna side by side, then the Buddha, then Kalki still to come, with sages and kings along the way.

teach.h: STREAMS FROM A LAKE THAT NEVER EMPTIES.
teach.b: Then it says the descents are beyond counting, like streams running without end from a lake that never empties. Now Jayadeva's hymn.

It does sing ten forms, and among them are Balarama with his plow, then the Buddha, then Kalki. Krishna isn't in his ten at all. That's because the whole hymn is sung to Krishna, as Keshava, the one who takes every form.
So one poet keeps both Balarama and the Buddha and lifts Krishna out of the line to stand behind it. Other lists, like Nani's, keep Krishna in the line and give the other place to Balarama.
Here's the puzzle, solved, and it's the Hindu teaching of the avatars at full size: God's coming down was never a closed set.

teach.h: TEN IS A FRAME, NOT A FENCE.
teach.b: Ten is a frame, not a fence. The tradition keeps the frame and lets more than one set of names stand inside it, and the Bhagavata itself says the lake was never going to fit on ten fingers.
Priya texts Dawa a photo of both lists. Dawa writes back: so nobody's list is wrong? Priya types: nobody's list is the whole lake.

how: Hindu families and temples count Vishnu's ten forms in more than one way; some lists include the Buddha and some Balarama, and Jayadeva's hymn of the ten is sung in some temples and homes.

o: the tenth form, still to come at the end of the age
in some lists of ten, Vishnu's ninth form; in others, absent
Balarama's other name, used in older lists of the ten

p: Balarama and the Buddha, sung to Krishna

s: every Hindu list of the ten forms is the same
some count the Buddha, some Balarama, and Jayadeva lifts Krishna out of the line.
the Bhagavata calls the descents beyond counting, like streams from an endless lake
he stands beside Krishna in the Bhagavata's list and in Jayadeva's ten.

games.q: Dawa asks: if Krishna isn't in Jayadeva's ten, did Jayadeva leave him out on purpose?
o: not to drop him: the whole hymn is sung to Krishna, the one who takes every form.
yes: Jayadeva honored Balarama and the Buddha more than Krishna.
yes: Krishna's stories weren't known yet when Jayadeva wrote.
games.why: Jayadeva's refrain addresses Keshava, Krishna, in every verse; Krishna stands behind the line of ten rather than in it.

practice: Count ten slowly on your fingers, any list you like, one breath for each finger, and let your hands fall open at ten.
Then keep sitting with your hands open, and let the breath run on past the count, like a stream that doesn't stop.

wordCard.voice: Buddha: counted among the ten in some Hindu lists and left out of others, where Balarama stands in his place.

orig.note: Sanskrit asankhyeya: beyond counting, the Bhagavata's word for the descents.

carryVoice: Your line: God's descents are beyond counting. The lake doesn't run dry, and no list of ten holds it all. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 1.3.23–26 (Balarama and Krishna; the Buddha; Kalki; the descents beyond counting, like streams from an unfailing lake)
Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, canto 1, the hymn of the ten forms (Balarama, Buddha, Kalki; sung to Keshava)
